title: Chapter 48: The Beguiling Boy 3
content:
Chapter 48

The final piece of Nie Mingjue’s corpse—his severed head—was indeed locked away in Jin Guangyao’s hands.

Back during the Sunshot Campaign, Chifeng-zun Nie Mingjue had charged through battlefields like an unstoppable force of nature, his wrath striking with the apocalyptic fury of rolling thunder. Yet here he was: smothered beneath heavy layers of binding talismans, locked away in the cramped gloom of a hidden vault, never to see the light of day again.

All Wei Wuxian had to do was crack the seal, and the rest of the corpse would catch the scent of its missing head and march over on its own. He studied the intricate wards encasing the helmet-like container, turning over a plan of attack in his head, when an overpowering suction tore through the chamber. The draft caught his weightless paper body like a dried leaf, violently dragging him forward until he smacked flat against Nie Mingjue’s forehead.

On the other side of Koi Tower, Lan Wangji sat perched by the daybed, his pale eyes fixed steadily on Wei Wuxian’s face. After a long, quiet vigil, his fingers twitched faintly. Lowering his lashes, he slowly raised a hand, brushing his fingertips across his own lips.

It was an impossibly light touch—as feather-soft as the accidental tap of a paper man’s head against his mouth.

Suddenly, Wei Wuxian’s hands shifted, his fingers curling into tight, white-knuckled fists. Lan Wangji’s gaze sharpened instantly. He leaned forward to cradle him against his chest, gently tilting his face up. Wei Wuxian’s eyes remained shut tight, but his brow was pinched into an agonizing, knotted furrow.

Deep inside the secret vault, Wei Wuxian hadn't even had a fraction of a second to brace himself. When a soul dies choking on monstrous resentment, that lingering wrath radiates outward in suffocating waves, lashing out at anyone nearby to vent its fury and drown them in its own agony. Most hauntings and spiritual rampages boiled down to this exact mechanism—which, in essence, was the foundational principle behind Empathy. Had Wei Wuxian been in his own flesh and blood, his physical body would have acted as a spiritual shield; as long as he kept his guard up, stray resentment couldn't easily breach his defenses. But tethered to a flimsy slip of paper, his spiritual resistance was gutted. Caught at point-blank range, the sheer volcanic mass of Nie Mingjue’s grudge swallowed him whole before he could even register the danger.

One second his brain was screamingabort, and the next, the coppery reek of hot blood flooded his senses.

It had been years since he’d smelled gore this thick. Something deep within his marrow snapped awake, roaring to a boil. When his vision cleared, the world erupted into a blur of flying steel and crimson spray, framed by a severed head spinning through the air and a heavy corpse dropping like a felled tree.

The fallen body wore the sunburst robes of the Qishan Wen Clan. Wei Wuxian watched as "his own" hands slid a massive saber smoothly back into its scabbard, a deep, gravelly voice rumbling from his chest: "Grab the head. String it up for the Wen dogs to see."

Behind him, a chorus of voices barked in unison, "Sir!"

Wei Wuxian recognized the dead man immediately.

Wen Xu, eldest son of the tyrant Wen Ruohan. Nie Mingjue had intercepted him in Hejian and taken his head in a single, brutal stroke, hoisting the severed prize high above the vanguard to shatter the enemy's nerve. As for the headless body, the vengeful Nie cultivators had hacked it to ribbons, grinding the remains into the dirt until nothing was left but a red smear.

Nie Mingjue cast a cold glance at the corpse, booted it aside, and rested a heavy palm on his saber hilt, slowly scanning the battlefield.

Chifeng-zun was a towering mountain of a man. When Wei Wuxian had channeled A-Qing's memories, his field of view had been comically low to the ground; now, he was looking down on the world from an altitude well above his own. Bodies littered the blood-soaked mud in every direction. A third wore the blazing sunburst robes of the Wen, a third bore the roaring beast-head crest of Qinghe Nie, and the rest were unmarked rogue cultivators. The carnage was absolute, the stench of slaughter thick enough to choke the heavens.

Nie Mingjue strode across the mud, hunting for any surviving Wen soldiers clinging to breath. A faint clatter echoed from inside a rundown cottage nearby. Without missing a beat, he slashed his saber through the air, sending a concussive blade of wind blowing the rotten wooden door clean off its hinges.

Cowering in the shadows were a terrified mother and child. The hovel was barren, offering no place to hide; the pair could only huddle beneath a splintered wooden table, clutching each other white-knuckled and barely daring to draw breath. The young mother’s wide eyes mirrored Nie Mingjue’s towering, blood-drenched silhouette, tears spilling down her cheeks in silent terror, while the little girl in her arms sat paralyzed with her mouth hanging open.

Realizing they were just ordinary civilians who hadn't evacuated before the slaughter broke out, the scowl between Nie Mingjue’s brows softened slightly. A subordinate hurried up behind him, taking in the scene with a cautious, "Sect Leader?"

To these peasants, life had been peaceful until groups of cultivators dropped out of the sky to turn their home into a bloodbath. They had no clue who was righteous and who was wicked; all they knew was that anyone carrying steel was an executioner, convinced their time had come. Nie Mingjue reined in his suffocating aura and said flatly, "You're safe."

He lowered his saber arm and walked on. Behind him, the young mother collapsed into the dirt, weeping in quiet relief.

After a few strides, Nie Mingjue paused. Without turning around, he asked, "Who was the last cultivator to pull back during the battlefield cleanup yesterday?"

The subordinate blinked, caught off guard. "The last one? Uh... I don't recall off the top of my head..."

Nie Mingjue’s brow furrowed. "Find out and report back."

He kept walking while the disciple scrambled off to ask around. A moment later, the man hurried back, breathless. "Sect Leader! I checked. The cultivator who stayed behind until the end was named Meng Yao."

Nie Mingjue arched an eyebrow, clearly surprised.

Wei Wuxian understood why. Before he’d been dragged into the golden fold of the Jin Clan, Jin Guangyao had gone by his mother's surname—Meng Yao. It was hardly a secret. In fact, back then, the name had been quite notorious.

Though few had witnessed Lianfang-zun’s very first attempt to climb Koi Tower, the rumors detailing his humiliation were common knowledge. His mother had been a famed courtesan in a high-end Yunmeng brothel, celebrated as an accomplished beauty of the pleasure quarters. Word was she played the zither exquisitely, wrote with elegant brushwork, and carried herself with the refined poise of an aristocratic lady. But in the eyes of society, a courtesan was still a whore. When Jin Guangshan’s wandering eye drifted through Yunmeng, he naturally couldn't resist a taste of the city's reigning jewel. He spent a few drunken days wrapped in her sheets, tossed her a token of affection, and strolled away thoroughly satisfied—promptly erasing her from his memory the second he crossed the city limits, just as he had done dozens of times before.

By comparison, Mo Xuanyu and his mother had practically hit the jackpot; at least Jin Guangshan had eventually remembered that boy existed and hauled him home. Meng Yao hadn't been so lucky. The son of a prostitute carried no weight against the child of a respectable household. Madame Meng raised the boy alone, clinging to the desperate hope that the great sect leader would return for them. She tutored Meng Yao meticulously, grooming him for the day he would enter the golden gates. But by the time the boy was an adolescent, no carriage had ever arrived, and his mother fell deathly ill.

On her deathbed, she pressed Jin Guangshan's old keepsake into her son's hands, telling him to seek his fortune at Koi Tower. Packing his bags, Meng Yao left Yunmeng on foot. He braved the long road to Lanling, only to be barred at the gates. Desperate, he pulled out the keepsake, begging the guards to send word.

That keepsake was a pearl button. In the Lanling Jin Sect, such trinkets were practically dirt—you could scoop them up by the handful. Jin Guangshan routinely used them to butter up pretty girls during his roadside flings, passing off cheap baubles as priceless heirlooms while whispering grand promises of eternity, only to forget the encounter before morning.

Meng Yao’s timing couldn't have been worse: it happened to be Jin Zixuan’s birthday. Jin Guangshan and Madame Jin were hosting an extravagant banquet for their prized golden heir, surrounded by clan elders and prestigious guests. Hours later, as the party prepared to step outside to release blessing lanterns, a servant finally found a gap to report the stranger at the gate. The moment Madame Jin laid eyes on that pearl button, all the humiliation from her husband's endless infidelities blew up in her face. Jin Guangshan panicked, grinding the pearl to dust beneath his heel while loudly screaming at the servant to run the beggar off before the guests caught sight of him.

And so, Meng Yao was kicked down Koi Tower’s towering staircase—tumbling over and over, from the very top step all the way to the bottom.

They said that when he finally scrambled to his feet, he didn't utter a word. He simply wiped the blood from his forehead, dusted off his coarse clothes, hoisted his pack, and walked away.

Once the Sunshot Campaign ignited, Meng Yao enlisted under the banner of the Qinghe Nie Sect.

Nie Mingjue’s forces were split across various encampments, with one outpost tucked away in an unnamed mountain range near Hejian. Trekking up the trail on foot, Nie Mingjue spotted a youth in coarse hemp stepping out from the dense emerald woods, carrying a bamboo water canteen.

The boy looked exhausted from the trek to the spring. He approached the mouth of a cave, but stopped dead in his tracks. Standing outside, he listened to the chatter within, hesitated, and quietly turned around, shuffling off in the opposite direction.

Settling by the roadside, he pulled a piece of dry ration from his tunic and chewed on it slowly, washing it down with cold water.

Nie Mingjue walked over. As his towering shadow fell across the dirt, the boy looked up, hurriedly tucking the dry bread away as he scrambled to his feet. "Sect Leader Nie."

The youth was slight of frame, with pale skin and soft, delicate brows—that same disarmingly polite face Jin Guangyao would wear for decades. At this point, he hadn't yet been recognized by the Jin clan, meaning his forehead was bare of the vermilion mark. Recognizing him, Nie Mingjue asked, "Meng Yao?"

Meng Yao bowed respectfully. "Yes, sir."

"Why aren't you resting inside with the others?"

Meng Yao parted his lips, flashing an awkward, strained smile, seemingly unsure how to answer. Frowning, Nie Mingjue pushed past him toward the cavern entrance. Meng Yao looked as if he wanted to hold him back, but didn't dare reach out. Moving without a sound, Nie Mingjue halted outside the mouth of the cave, where the boisterous jeers from within carried loud and clear:

"...Yeah, that's him."

"No way! Jin Guangshan’s kid? Why would a sect leader's son be slumming it in the mud with us? Why doesn't he go run home to daddy? A snap of his fingers and he'd never have to break a sweat again."

"You think he didn't try? The bastard hauled that token all the way from Yunmeng to Lanling, practically begging to be claimed!"

"Well, he miscalculated. Madame Jin is terrifying."

"Honestly, Jin Guangshan has bastards scattered all over the place—at least a dozen of them. Has he ever acknowledged a single one? Bringing all that shame on himself, he got what was coming to him."

"People shouldn't reach for things they have no right to touch. Cracking your skull on the pavement? Can't blame anyone but yourself. Brought it right on his own head."

"Idiots! With Jin Zixuan around, why would Jin Guangshan give a damn about any other boy? Especially one birthed by a common street whore who’s been ridden by thousands! Who the hell knows whose seed he actually is? Ten to one, Jin Guangshan was too spooked by the taint to claim him! Hahaha!"

"As if! He probably forgot he ever touched the woman to begin with."

"I gotta admit, knowing Jin Guangshan’s get is stuck hauling water for us like a dog feels pretty damn sweet, haha..."

"Like hell he's accepted his lot! Haven't you seen him sucking up to everyone? Running around like a busy little bee, desperate to make a name for himself so his dear old dad might throw him a bone."

A flash of white-hot fury flared in Nie Mingjue’s chest, the heat searing straight through Wei Wuxian’s borrowed senses.

Nie Mingjue’s hand clamped down on his saber hilt. Meng Yao lunged to stop him, but it was too late. The blade cleared its sheath, and a concussive blast of spiritual energy sent an enormous boulder crashing down before the cave mouth. The disciples resting inside scrambled to their feet in sheer terror, drawing their steel as bamboo canteens clattered across the stone.

Nie Mingjue’s roar shook the mountain: "You drink the water he hauled up the mountain, yet spit vile poison behind his back! Did you enlist under my command to cut down Wen dogs, or to flap your filthy jaws?!"

The cave descended into absolute, panicked silence. Everyone knew Chifeng-zun’s temper; the more you made excuses, the harder the disciplinary flogging would be. Nobody dared utter a squeak. Nie Mingjue let out a harsh scoff, refusing to even step inside. Turning to Meng Yao, he commanded, "Come with me."

He marched down the path, and Meng Yao scrambled to trail behind. The further they walked, the lower Meng Yao hung his head, his steps dragging with heavy hesitation.

Finally, the youth murmured, "Thank you, Sect Leader Nie."

Nie Mingjue replied bluntly, "A real man stands tall and walks upright. Pay no mind to the barking of idle fools."

Meng Yao dipped his chin. "Yes, sir."

Though he answered obediently, a dark veil of worry still clouded his brow. Nie Mingjue’s defense had quelled the sneers for today, but the moment his back was turned, those cultivators would make Meng Yao pay for it tenfold. How could he not worry?

Nie Mingjue continued, "The louder they sneer behind your back, the harder you must work to leave them utterly speechless. I’ve watched you on the field. You are always at the vanguard, and you are always the last to leave so you can evacuate the civilians. You have done well. Keep at it."

Meng Yao froze, his head lifting slightly in disbelief.

"Your swordplay is agile, but lacks a solid foundation. Train harder."

It was an open, honest compliment. Meng Yao bowed deeply. "Thank you for the guidance, Sect Leader Nie!"

Wei Wuxian, however, knew the truth: no amount of training was ever going to fix that foundation. Unlike heirs raised on top-tier clan elixirs, Meng Yao’s spiritual baseline was abysmal. He could never reach the pinnacle of pure martial power, leaving him no choice but to broaden his repertoire rather than master a single discipline. That was why he studied the secret techniques of every clan he could get his hands on—and why the sects would later brand him a thief of martial arts.

Hejian was a vital strategic stronghold during the war—Nie Mingjue’s primary theater. His forces acted as an iron wall, preventing the Qishan Wen Clan from pressing south or expanding east. The Nie and Wen clans had shared deep blood feuds for generations, and with the war underway, the clashes were brutal, relentless meat grinders. The commoners caught in the crossfire suffered horribly. The Wen Clan butchered without a second thought, but the Qinghe Nie Clan could not afford such callousness.

Under these circumstances, Meng Yao’s tireless efforts to clean up the wreckage and shield the refugees caught Nie Mingjue’s eye. After several campaigns, Nie Mingjue promoted him directly to serve as his personal adjutant. Meng Yao seized the opportunity with both hands, executing every single order with razor-sharp efficiency. Back then, far from barking at him, Nie Mingjue held him in high esteem. Having heard endless jokes about how Lianfang-zun ran away with his tail between his legs whenever Chifeng-zun came around, watching them get along like grease and fire felt surreal to Wei Wuxian.

One day, the Hejian outpost welcomed an esteemed guest.

During the Sunshot Campaign, the Three Zuns each carved their own legends. Chifeng-zun Nie Mingjue was an unstoppable butcher, clearing every field until not a single Wen dog remained breathing. Ze-wu-jun Lan Xichen was different: with Gusu firmly held by Lan Qiren, he spent his days riding to the rescue of beleaguered clans, pulling allies out of the jaws of death and reclaiming lost ground countless times. People rejoiced at the mere mention of his name, viewing his arrival as a divine lifeline.

Whenever Lan Xichen escorted retreating cultivators through Hejian, he would use the outpost as a staging ground. Nie Mingjue welcomed him into a spacious hall where several clan leaders sat gathered.

Though Lan Xichen looked nearly identical to Lan Wangji, Wei Wuxian could tell them apart in a heartbeat. Still, catching sight of that face made his heart twitch, wondering:How is my physical body doing right now? Did the resentment hitting my paper vessel cause a backlash in the flesh? Did Lan Zhan notice something's wrong?

After trading brief pleasantries, Meng Yao, who had been standing quietly behind Nie Mingjue, stepped forward to serve tea. Out on the frontlines, every soldier pulled the weight of six men, leaving no room for servants or maids; Meng Yao had taken all those domestic chores onto his own shoulders. When the visiting cultivators recognized his face, their expressions shifted into awkward contempt. Gossip about Jin Guangshan’s scandalous escapades had always traveled fast, and Meng Yao had been a laughingstock for months. Convinced the son of a whore was tainted, several clan leaders set their teacups aside untouched, pointedly taking out white handkerchiefs to scrub their fingertips as if scrubbing off filth. Nie Mingjue was too blunt to notice such petty slights, but Wei Wuxian caught the gesture out of the corner of his eye.

Meng Yao acted as if he hadn't seen a thing, his warm, polite smile never slipping for a second as he continued serving. When he reached Lan Xichen, the young master looked up with a gentle smile. "Thank you."

Lan Xichen took a sip from his cup before turning back to converse with Nie Mingjue, leaving the snobbish cultivators shifting uncomfortably in their seats.

Nie Mingjue, rarely one for idle smiles, softened his tone for Lan Xichen. "How long can you stay?"

"I must trouble you for a single night," Lan Xichen replied. "Tomorrow, I depart to link up with Wangji."

"Where is he?"

"Jiangling."

Nie Mingjue frowned. "Isn't Jiangling still held by the Wen dogs?"

"Not as of two days ago," Lan Xichen said. "It is now under the control of the Yunmeng Jiang Clan."

A guest sect leader piped up, "Sect Leader Nie might not know, but young Sect Leader Jiang has been cutting quite the figure in that region lately."

Another sneered quietly, "How could he not? With Wei Wuxian fighting like an army of a million men, who does he have to fear? He doesn't have to scramble for his life like the rest of us; he just sits comfortably in his stronghold. Some people really have all the luck..."

Sensing the bitterness brewing, someone hastily cut in, "Ah, it is all thanks to Ze-wu-jun and Hanguang-jun running support across the realm, otherwise countless clans would have been slaughtered by now."

Nie Mingjue turned back to Lan Xichen. "Your brother is in Jiangling?"

"Yes. He took a detachment there early in the month."

"Your brother's cultivation is peerless; he is more than enough on his own. Why are you heading there?"

Hearing Nie Mingjue praise Lan Wangji’s martial prowess filled Wei Wuxian with an absurd swell of pride:Chifeng-zun has great taste!

Lan Xichen let out a quiet sigh. "To be frank, ever since Wangji arrived, he and Young Master Wei of the Jiang Clan have had quite a bit of friction. I felt it best to check on them."

Nie Mingjue raised a brow. "Friction over what?"

A cultivator chimed in, "Word is Hanguang-jun took issue with Wei Wuxian's heretical methods. Rumor has it he publicly chewed him out—calling him out for desecrating corpses, reveling in slaughter, and losing his mind. Though people are treating Wei Wuxian like a god of war after the battle of Jiangling; I'd love to see his craft with my own eyes."

That was putting it politely; back then, rumors flew that he and Lan Wangji were trading blows mid-battle while slaying Wen soldiers. In truth, their relationship hadn't been quite as hostile as the tavern gossip made it out to be, though there had certainly been friction. During that period, Wei Wuxian had spent every night digging up graves, and Lan Wangji had never missed a chance to lecture him—claiming it corrupted the body and soul, even drawing his sword to block him. With bloody skirmishes breaking out every few days, tempers on both sides were razor-thin, and their talks inevitably ended in shouting matches. Listening to strangers discuss it now felt like a lifetime ago—and Wei Wuxian caught himself with a bitter jolt:Right. It literally was a lifetime ago.

A guest leader muttered, "Honestly, Hanguang-jun is being far too rigid. The living are dying by the thousands; who has the luxury to worry about the dignity of dead bodies?"

Another agreed, "Desperate times call for desperate measures. Sect Leader Jiang had it right: who could be more wicked than the Wen dogs? As long as he's on our side and butchering the enemy, that's all that matters."

Funny,Wei Wuxian thought dryly.You singing a different tune when you all sieged the Burial Mounds to tear me apart.

Soon after, Lan Xichen rose to lead his men to their quarters, with Meng Yao guiding the way. Nie Mingjue returned to his room, retrieved an elegant saber, and set out to find Lan Xichen.

Before he reached the door, hushed voices filtered through the lattice. Lan Xichen was saying, "What a coincidence that you ended up serving as Mingjue-xiong's adjutant."

Meng Yao replied, "It is entirely thanks to Chifeng-zun's grace and favor."

Lan Xichen smiled. "Mingjue-xiong's temper is like fire; earning his trust is no small feat." He paused before adding gently, "Lately, Sect Leader Jin has been struggling on the Langya front and is recruiting talent."

Meng Yao hesitated. "Ze-wu-jun, you mean..."

"You need not be so formal with me. I remember you once told me that your deepest wish was to secure a place in the Lanling Jin Clan and earn your father's acknowledgment. Now that you have proven yourself under Mingjue-xiong, does that wish still stand?"

Meng Yao fell silent. After an agonizing pause, he whispered, "...It does."

"I thought as much."

Meng Yao murmured, "Yet I am already Sect Leader Nie's adjutant. He showed me kindness when I had nothing. Regardless of what I desire, I cannot abandon Hejian."

Lan Xichen considered this. "True. It would be awkward for you to bring it up. But I believe that if you ask, Mingjue-xiong will respect your choice. Should he refuse, I can speak on your behalf."

"Why would I refuse?"

Nie Mingjue shoved the door open. Lan Xichen and Meng Yao were seated across from each other, looking startled. Meng Yao sprang to his feet, but before he could speak, Nie Mingjue snapped, "Sit down."

Meng Yao froze. Nie Mingjue continued, "Tomorrow, I will draft a letter of recommendation for you."

"Sect Leader Nie?"

"You may take the letter to Langya and find your father."

Meng Yao stammered, "Sect Leader Nie, if you heard our conversation, you must have heard me say—"

"I promoted you because you are capable, and because your conduct met my standards—not so you could spend your life repaying a debt! If you truly wish to repay me, go slay a few more Wen dogs on the battlefield!"

The silver-tongued Meng Yao was struck entirely dumb. Lan Xichen smiled. "See? I told you Mingjue-xiong would understand."

Tears welled in Meng Yao’s eyes. "Sect Leader Nie, Ze-wu-jun... I..." Lowering his head, he choked out, "...I truly do not know what to say."

Nie Mingjue sat down. "If you don't know what to say, then keep your mouth shut."

He placed the slender saber onto the table. Lan Xichen’s eyes lit up. "Huaisang's saber?"

"He may be safe under your roof, but he cannot slack off on his training. Have your men keep an eye on him; next time I see him, I'm testing his saber forms."

Lan Xichen laughed. "He used to claim he'd left his saber at home; now he has no excuses left."

Nie Mingjue looked between them. "By the way... had you two met before?"

Meng Yao nodded. "I had the privilege of meeting Ze-wu-jun once."

"Where? When?"

Lan Xichen waved his hands with an embarrassed laugh. "Let us leave that unsaid. It was the greatest humiliation of my life—Mingjue-xiong, please do not pry."

"What is there to hide from me? Meng Yao, speak."

Meng Yao offered a diplomatic smile. "If Ze-wu-jun wishes to keep it private, I must keep his secret."

The three of them traded banter, shifting between war logistics and casual teasing, the atmosphere infinitely warmer than the stiff reception hall earlier. Watching them, Wei Wuxian caught himself itching to chime in, thinking:Their bond was genuinely strong back then. Ze-wu-jun is so easy to talk to—how did Lan Zhan end up so painfully taciturn? Then again, Lan Zhan's stoic silence is nice in its own way; I do all the talking, and he just listens and drops a quiet "Mm". What do they call that again...?

A few days later, Meng Yao departed Hejian for Langya, clutching Nie Mingjue’s recommendation.

Nie Mingjue appointed a replacement adjutant, but to Wei Wuxian’s borrowed senses, the newcomer was perpetually half a step too slow. Meng Yao had been a rare talent—catching unsaid cues, turning a three-word instruction into flawless execution without dragging his feet. Once you were spoiled by someone that competent, working with anyone else was an exercise in frustration.

Weeks later, the Lanling Jin forces on the Langya front were on the verge of collapse. With Lan Xichen deployed elsewhere, Jin Guangshan sent an urgent plea for help to Hejian, and Nie Mingjue marched to his aid.

Once the skirmish cleared, a frazzled Jin Guangshan came over to offer his thanks. After trading brief pleasantries, Nie Mingjue cut to the chase: "Sect Leader Jin, what duties has Meng Yao been assigned lately?"

Jin Guangshan blinked. "Meng Yao? Ah... pardon my ignorance, Sect Leader Nie, but who might that be?"

Nie Mingjue’s scowl deepened instantly. The spectacle of Meng Yao being kicked down Koi Tower’s stairs had been tavern fodder for months; there was no way the man responsible had forgotten the name. Anyone with a shred of shame wouldn't dare feign ignorance, but Jin Guangshan’s skin was thicker than a fortress wall.

Nie Mingjue’s voice turned icy. "Meng Yao was my personal adjutant. I sent him to you with a letter of recommendation."

Jin Guangshan kept playing the fool. "Truly? I have seen no such letter, nor have I seen the boy. Had I known Sect Leader Nie dispatched an adjutant, I would have received him with the highest honors. Could there have been a misunderstanding?"

He brushed it off, claiming he’d never heard of the person. Disgusted by the brazen lies, Nie Mingjue took his leave without another word. He questioned several Jin disciples, turning up nothing, and wandered through the camp until his boots carried him toward a secluded grove.

The woods were dead quiet, still bearing the fresh scars of an ambush. The ground was littered with corpses clad in the robes of the Wen, Jin, and minor allied clans.

A wet, sickening squelch broke the silence ahead.

Nie Mingjue rested his hand on his saber, slipping through the trees. Parting the branches, his eyes locked onto Meng Yao standing amidst the carnage. With a flick of his wrist, the youth smoothly withdrew a sword from the chest of a fallen cultivator.

His face was an eerie mask of absolute calm, his strike swift, steady, and terrifyingly precise—not a single drop of blood staining his robes.

The weapon in his grip wasn't his own; the guard was decorated with iron sunbursts—a Wen sword.

The technique he’d just used was a Wen sword form.

And the man dead at his feet wore the Sparks Amidst Snow robes of the Lanling Jin Clan.

Nie Mingjue didn't say a word. His saber shifted an inch from its sheath, releasing a razor-sharp metallic ring.

At that familiar sound, Meng Yao violently flinched. He spun around, the color draining from his face as his soul nearly left his body: "...Sect Leader Nie?"

Nie Mingjue drew his saber completely. The steel gleamed snow-white, though a faint, sinister crimson aura bled along the edge. Wei Wuxian could feel the volcanic, suffocating wrath radiating through the man’s bones, tangled with searing disappointment and bitter hatred.

Knowing Nie Mingjue’s unyielding code better than anyone, Meng Yao dropped the sword with a loud clatter. "Sect Leader Nie! Please, wait! Hear me out!"

Nie Mingjue’s roar shook the leaves: "What is there to explain?!"

Meng Yao scrambled forward on his knees. "I had no choice! I was forced into this!"

"Forced?! What did I tell you when I sent you here?!"

Meng Yao prostrated himself at his boots. "Sect Leader Nie, listen to me! This man was my superior officer. He looked down on me from the start, beating and humiliating me at every turn..."

"So you murdered him?!"

"No! Not because of that! I can endure beatings and insults—I've endured them my entire life! But every time we captured a Wen outpost, every plan I painstakingly drafted, every charge I led on the frontlines—he would claim all the credit with a single stroke of his brush, claiming I did nothing! It wasn't the first time; it happened every single time! I tried reasoning with him, but he laughed in my face. I went to the others, but no one would listen to a word I said! And just now... he mocked my mother, calling her a... I lost my head, I lost control, and my hand slipped!"

Terrified that Nie Mingjue’s blade would sever his neck before he finished, Meng Yao spoke at a frantic clip. Yet even in his panic, his narrative was impeccably structured—highlighting the victim's cruelty while casting himself as the helpless victim.

Nie Mingjue seized him by the collar, hauling him off his knees. "You lie!"

Meng Yao shuddered. Nie Mingjue stared into his eyes, his voice dropping low and venomous: "You lost control in a fit of rage? Does a man who lost control wear the chilling expression you wore just now? Would he deliberately pick a secluded grove fresh from an ambush? Would he specifically use a Wen sword and Wen forms to frame an enemy sneak attack?! You calculated this from the start!"

Meng Yao raised a trembling hand. "I swear it! Every word is the truth!"

"Even if it were, you had no right to take his life! A bit of battlefield glory—is petty vanity worth so much to you?!"

Meng Yao froze. "A bit of battlefield glory...?"

His voice trembled, hollow and cracked. "...What do you mean, 'a bit of glory'? Chifeng-zun, do you have any idea how much blood I bled for that glory?! Vanity?! Without that vanity, I am nothing!"

Looking down at the youth weeping and trembling before him—in stark, terrifying contrast to the cold-blooded executioner from moments before—Nie Mingjue found the whiplash sickening.

"Meng Yao, answer me: when I first met you outside that cave, did you stage that pathetic, bullied routine on purpose so I would stand up for you? If I hadn't stepped in, would you have slaughtered those disciples just like this?"

Meng Yao’s throat bobbed, cold sweat dripping down his temple. He opened his mouth, but Nie Mingjue barked: "Do not dare lie to my face!"

Meng Yao flinched, swallowing the excuse whole. Collapsing back to his knees, his fingers clawed deep into the mud.

After an agonizing silence, Nie Mingjue slid his saber slowly back into its sheath. "I will not execute you myself."

Meng Yao’s head snapped up.

"Go turn yourself in to the Lanling Jin Clan. Take whatever punishment they see fit."

Meng Yao went rigid. "...Chifeng-zun, I cannot fall here."

"You took a crooked step."

"You are sentencing me to death."

"If your claims hold true, they will not kill you. Go, and reflect on your sins."

Meng Yao whispered, "...My father hasn't even acknowledged me yet."

Jin Guangshan hadn't failed to see him. He simply chose to pretend the boy didn't exist.

Crushed beneath Nie Mingjue’s suffocating aura, Meng Yao finally squeezed out a weak, compliant, "Yes, sir."

"Get up."

As if drained of all strength, Meng Yao stumbled to his feet, swaying on his legs. Seeing him stumble, Nie Mingjue reached out to steady him. Meng Yao murmured, "...Thank you, Sect Leader Nie."

Watching him look so utterly broken, Nie Mingjue turned to leave.

Behind him, a faint whisper rasped: "...I still cannot."

Nie Mingjue whipped around—and saw Meng Yao holding a drawn blade.

The tip was pressed flush against his own stomach. With a look of hollow despair, Meng Yao cried, "Sect Leader Nie, I have failed your kindness!"

He drove the blade inward. Nie Mingjue’s pupils contracted, lunging to knock the weapon aside, but it was too late. The steel punched clean through Meng Yao’s abdomen, bursting out through his spine as his body crumpled into the pool of blood.

Shocked, Nie Mingjue dropped to one knee, turning the boy over. "What have you done...?!"

Meng Yao’s face was deathly pale, his lips curling into a weak, bitter smile. "Sect Leader Nie... I..."

His head lolled sideways. Supporting his frame while avoiding the blade, Nie Mingjue pressed a palm to his heart, funneling a steady stream of spiritual energy into his core.

Suddenly, a violent jolt wracked Nie Mingjue’s meridians as an icy, venomous flow of dark spiritual needles erupted from the youth's abdomen, paralyzing his core!

Wei Wuxian, having anticipated a trick, wasn't surprised. But Nie Mingjue had never imagined Meng Yao would dare strike him down in cold blood. As he knelt paralyzed, watching Meng Yao casually climb back to his feet, the shock in his chest far eclipsed his rage.

Meng Yao had calculated the angle with surgical precision, avoiding every vital organ. With practiced ease, he drew the longsword from his own gut, flicking the crimson blade clean before pressing a firm hand against the wound to staunch the flow.

Nie Mingjue remained frozen in his kneeling stance, his chin slightly lifted, staring him down.

Neither man uttered a word. Meng Yao sheathed his sword, offered a deep, formal bow, and vanished into the timber without looking back.

To confess obediently, feign a suicidal breakdown, deliver a paralyzing ambush, and vanish into thin air—Nie Mingjue had never witnessed such shameless treachery in his life, let alone from a trusted adjutant he had personally groomed.

His fury detonated, unleashing unprecedented savagery on the Wen forces over the following days. When Lan Xichen arrived in Langya with reinforcements a few days later, Nie Mingjue’s temper was still at a rolling boil.

Lan Xichen teased with an easy smile, "Mingjue-xiong's fire burns as bright as ever. Where is Meng Yao? Has he not come to pour cold water on your temper?"

"Never speak that name in my presence again!"

Nie Mingjue recounted the entire betrayal—the framed murder, the fake suicide, the cowardly ambush. Lan Xichen stood frozen in disbelief. "How could this be? Could there be a misunderstanding?"

"I caught him red-handed! What misunderstanding could there be?!"

Lan Xichen murmured thoughtfully, "From his account, the man he killed was certainly in the wrong, though taking his life was inexcusable. In times of war, judgment is difficult. Where has he gone now?"

Nie Mingjue’s voice was like grinding iron: "He had better pray he never crosses my path again, or I will feed his blood to my saber!"

Yet those words proved an empty promise. Over the following years, Meng Yao seemed to evaporate from the face of the earth, leaving behind not a single trace.

The deeper Nie Mingjue’s initial admiration had been, the more toxic his revulsion became. Whenever the name arose, his face clouded over with bitter disgust, until eventually he refused to speak of the traitor entirely.

Nie Mingjue rarely let people close to his heart. To finally find an adjutant he trusted implicitly—valuing both his intellect and his character—only to realize the man was a duplicitous viper... it was no wonder the wound had never healed.

While Wei Wuxian turned these memories over, a blinding, skull-splitting agony tore through his head. Every bone in his body felt as though it had been crushed beneath an iron war chariot, grinding together with sickening creaks at the slightest twitch.

Forcing his eyes open, his vision swam, barely registering a massive hall paved in freezing black jade, strewn with sprawling, unconscious silhouettes. Nie Mingjue’s skull was battered, the wounds numb and crusted with dried blood across his brow and lashes. A faint shift of his neck sent fresh, warm crimson trickling into his eye.

Wei Wuxian’s breath hitched.

Nie Mingjue had been an unstoppable titan during the war; enemies could barely graze his robes, let alone leave him battered like a broken ragdoll.

What happened here?!

A soft rustle broke the silence. Glancing sideways, Wei Wuxian caught blurred shapes draped in sunburst robes. They were crawling forward across the black stone on their knees with practiced, terrified deference.

Wei Wuxian went dead quiet.

A suffocating, bone-chilling pressure descended over the chamber, rippling through Nie Mingjue’s shattered frame straight into Wei Wuxian’s soul. Lifting his heavy gaze, he saw a colossal jade throne perched at the far end of the hall.

A man sat upon it.

Blinded by blood and distance, Nie Mingjue couldn't make out the features, but he didn't need to. There was only one man who ruled from that throne.

The palace doors creaked open, and a solitary figure stepped over the threshold.

While the surrounding disciples crawled like worms, this arrival offered a brief, formal bow at the entrance, then casually strolled down the long black jade corridor without an ounce of hesitation. Reaching the dais, he leaned close, listening as the tyrant murmured a few quiet orders, before turning around to face the hall.

He ambled down the steps, stopping before the battered, defiant form of Nie Mingjue.

Studying the blood-soaked titan, a gentle, polite smile curled on his lips.

"Sect Leader Nie. Long time no see."

That voice... who else could it be but Meng Yao?
